title: Proteins, Enzymes & Biomolecules
description: Amino acids and their properties, peptide bonds, protein structure and folding, hemoglobin and myoglobin, enzyme kinetics and inhibition, carbohydrates, lipids, membranes and nucleic acids.

cards.title: What is the net form of a free amino acid with no ionizable side chain near its isoelectric point?
cards.body:
A **zwitterion**: $\ce{-NH3+}$ and $\ce{-COO-}$ on the same molecule, net charge $0$.

At pH 7 the $\alpha$-carboxyl (pKa about 2) is deprotonated and the $\alpha$-amino group (pKa about 9 to 10) is protonated.

Why: amino acids are crystalline, high-melting solids that dissolve well in water, not like neutral amines or acids.
Watch out: a zwitterion has both charges but a net charge of zero, so it is not the same as an uncharged molecule.
cards.searchQuery: amino acid zwitterion isoelectric point

cards.title: Which of the 20 standard amino acids is achiral?
cards.body:
Glycine

Its side chain is $\ce{H}$, so the $\alpha$-carbon has two identical hydrogens and no stereocenter.

Key idea: every other standard amino acid is chiral, and those in proteins are the **L** form.
cards.searchQuery: glycine only achiral amino acid

cards.title: Almost all L-amino acids are $S$. Which one is $R$ even though it is an L-amino acid?
cards.body:
Cysteine

Its $\ce{-CH2SH}$ side chain outranks $\ce{-COOH}$ in the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priorities because sulfur has a higher atomic number than oxygen.

Why: the spatial arrangement matches the other L-amino acids; only the priority order changes the label.
Watch out: L/D describes configuration relative to glyceraldehyde; $R/S$ is a separate system.
cards.searchQuery: cysteine R configuration L-amino acid CIP priority

cards.title: Roughly what pKa values do the $\alpha$-carboxyl and $\alpha$-amino groups of a free amino acid have?
cards.body:
About $2$ for $\alpha\text{-}\ce{COOH}$ and about $9$ to $10$ for $\alpha\text{-}\ce{NH3+}$.

The nearby positive ammonium lowers the carboxyl pKa compared with acetic acid (about 4.8).

Example: at pH 7 both groups are ionized, giving the zwitterion.
Tip: at pH above the amino pKa the group loses its proton and the molecule becomes an anion.
cards.searchQuery: amino acid alpha carboxyl amino pKa values

cards.title: Glycine has pKa values of $2.3$ and $9.6$. What is its pI? (one decimal, number only)
cards.body:
$6.0$

For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, $\mathrm{pI} = \frac{pK_1 + pK_2}{2}$.

$\frac{2.3 + 9.6}{2} = 5.95 \approx 6.0$

Why: pI is the pH of net zero charge, midway between the two pKa values that bracket the neutral zwitterion.
cards.searchQuery: calculate isoelectric point glycine pKa

cards.title: Aspartate has pKa values of $2.0$ ($\alpha$-COOH), $3.9$ (side chain) and $9.9$ ($\alpha$-NH$_3^+$). What is its pI? (two decimals, number only)
cards.body:
$2.95$

For an acidic amino acid, average the two **lowest** pKa values, since the neutral form sits between them: $\frac{2.0 + 3.9}{2} = 2.95$.

Watch out: do not include $9.9$; that deprotonation happens long after the net charge has become negative.
cards.searchQuery: isoelectric point aspartic acid calculation acidic amino acid

cards.title: Lysine has pKa values of $2.2$, $9.0$ and $10.5$ (side chain). What is its pI? (two decimals, number only)
cards.body:
$9.75$

For a basic amino acid, average the two **highest** pKa values: $\frac{9.0 + 10.5}{2} = 9.75$.

Tip: draw the charge ladder $+2, +1, 0, -1$ and place pI between the two pKa values that surround the $0$ species.
cards.searchQuery: isoelectric point lysine basic amino acid calculation

cards.title: Why is histidine so often found in enzyme active sites as an acid-base catalyst?
cards.body:
Its imidazole side chain has a pKa near $6$, so at physiological pH it can both donate and accept protons.

No other standard side chain has a pKa this close to $7$.

Example: His57 in chymotrypsin acts as a general base to activate the serine nucleophile.
Key idea: **histidine** is the only residue that is partly protonated near pH 7.
cards.searchQuery: histidine imidazole pKa 6 acid base catalysis active site

cards.title: A weak acid has pKa $6.4$. What is the ratio $[\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]$ at pH $7.4$? (number only)
cards.body:
$10$

Henderson-Hasselbalch: $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$.

$7.4 = 6.4 + \log R$, so $\log R = 1$ and $R = 10$.

Tip: every pH unit away from the pKa changes the ratio by a factor of $10$; at pH = pKa it is $1$.
cards.searchQuery: Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio conjugate base weak acid

cards.title: Which amino acid contributes most to a protein's absorbance at $280$ nm?
cards.body:
Tryptophan

Its indole ring has the largest extinction coefficient at 280 nm, followed by tyrosine; phenylalanine absorbs only weakly near 257 nm.

Why: a protein lacking Trp and Tyr gives almost no $A_{280}$ signal, so concentration estimates can be wrong.
Tip: $A_{280}$ also picks up nucleic acid contamination, which absorbs at 260 nm.
cards.searchQuery: tryptophan absorbance 280 nm protein concentration

cards.title: What is the one-letter code for tryptophan?
cards.body:
W

The most distinctive letter assignment; it resembles the double-ring shape of the indole group.

Mnemonic: **W**-ow, the huge double-ring side chain.
cards.searchQuery: tryptophan one letter code W amino acid

cards.title: What is the one-letter code for glutamine?
cards.body:
Q

Glutamine is Q, glutamate (glutamic acid) is E, asparagine is N and aspartate is D.

Mnemonic: **Q**-tamine, glutamine; glutamate sounds like **E**-glutamate.
cards.searchQuery: glutamine one letter code Q amino acid

cards.title: What is the one-letter code for lysine?
cards.body:
K

Arginine is R and histidine is H, the other basic residues.

Mnemonic: L is taken by leucine, so lysine gets the letter near it in its name, **K** (as in "lysKine").
cards.searchQuery: lysine one letter code K amino acid

cards.title: What structural feature makes proline unique among the standard amino acids?
cards.body:
Its side chain loops back and bonds to the backbone nitrogen, forming a **pyrrolidine ring**.

The $\alpha$-nitrogen is a secondary amine, so it has no N-H to donate in a helix and the $\phi$ angle is locked near $-65^\circ$.

Why: that rigidity disrupts $\alpha$-helices and $\beta$-sheets and makes proline common in turns.
Watch out: proline is an imino acid in older terminology, but it is still an $\alpha$-amino acid by modern definition.
cards.searchQuery: proline pyrrolidine ring secondary amine helix breaker

cards.title: Two cysteine side chains oxidize to form a disulfide bond. What is the oxidized dimer called?
cards.body:
Cystine

The reaction is $\ce{2 R-SH -> R-S-S-R + 2H+ + 2e-}$.

Why: disulfides are common in secreted, extracellular proteins such as insulin and antibodies; the cytosol is reducing (high glutathione), so disulfides are rare there.
Watch out: cysteine is the single residue, cystine is the oxidized dimer.
cards.searchQuery: cystine disulfide bond cysteine oxidation protein

cards.title: Which vitamin is a cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, the enzyme that makes hydroxyproline in collagen?
cards.body:
Vitamin C (ascorbate)

Ascorbate keeps the active-site iron in the Fe$^{2+}$ state.

Why: without hydroxyproline, collagen triple helices are unstable and tissues weaken, the basis of **scurvy**.
Example: scurvy shows as bleeding gums, poor wound healing and fragile blood vessels.
cards.searchQuery: vitamin C prolyl hydroxylase collagen scurvy

cards.title: Name the nine essential amino acids for adult humans.
cards.body:
His, Ile, Leu, Lys, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp, Val

Humans lack the pathways to make them, so they must come from the diet.

Mnemonic: **PVT TIM HALL** (Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg, Leu, Lys).
Watch out: this mnemonic includes Arg, which is only conditionally essential (needed during growth), so the strict adult list is the other nine.
cards.searchQuery: nine essential amino acids list humans

cards.title: Which standard amino acids carry a charged side chain at pH 7?
cards.body:
Negative: Asp and Glu. Positive: Lys and Arg (His is partly protonated).

The acidic side chains have pKa near $4$, while Lys is near $10.5$ and Arg near $12.5$.

Key idea: **Arg** has the highest side-chain pKa, so it stays positive over almost the whole physiological range.
cards.searchQuery: charged amino acids acidic basic side chains pKa

cards.title: Which "21st amino acid" is encoded by a UGA codon in a special context?
cards.body:
Selenocysteine

It is cysteine with selenium in place of sulfur and needs its own tRNA and an SECIS element in the mRNA.

Example: glutathione peroxidase and thioredoxin reductase contain selenocysteine at the active site.
cards.searchQuery: selenocysteine 21st amino acid UGA codon

cards.title: Which three amino acids are phosphorylated by protein kinases in eukaryotes?
cards.body:
Serine, threonine and tyrosine

All three have a side-chain $\ce{-OH}$ that accepts a phosphate from ATP.

Why: phosphorylation adds two negative charges, which can change conformation and create binding sites.
Watch out: histidine, aspartate and lysine are phosphorylated in bacterial signaling or special cases, but the $\ce{-OH}$ trio dominates in eukaryotes.
cards.searchQuery: protein phosphorylation serine threonine tyrosine kinase

cards.title: Which two standard amino acids contain sulfur?
cards.body:
Cysteine and methionine

Cys has a thiol $\ce{-SH}$; Met has a thioether $\ce{-S-CH3}$ and is the usual start residue.

Key idea: only **Cys** can form disulfide bonds.
cards.searchQuery: sulfur containing amino acids cysteine methionine

cards.title: Why is the peptide bond planar and not free to rotate?
cards.body:
Resonance gives the C-N bond about $40\%$ **double-bond character**.

So the six atoms $\mathrm{C}_\alpha$, C, O, N, H and the next $\mathrm{C}_\alpha$ lie in one plane, usually in the **trans** arrangement.

Why: only the $\phi$ (N-C$_\alpha$) and $\psi$ (C$_\alpha$-C) bonds rotate, which is what a Ramachandran plot shows.
Watch out: the C-N bond length (about $1.33\,\mathrm{\AA}$) is between single and double.
cards.searchQuery: peptide bond planar partial double bond resonance

cards.title: Which peptide bonds are found in the cis form far more often than the usual trans form?
cards.body:
Those preceding proline (Xaa-Pro bonds), about $5\%$ cis.

For most residues the cis form is well under $1\%$, because cis puts the side chains of neighboring residues in a steric clash.

Why: proline's ring makes cis and trans similar in energy.
Example: **peptidyl-prolyl isomerases** such as cyclophilin speed up cis-trans interconversion, a slow step in folding.
cards.searchQuery: cis proline peptide bond prolyl isomerase folding

cards.title: How many peptide bonds are in a linear polypeptide of $50$ residues? (number only)
cards.body:
49

Each bond joins two neighboring residues, so $n$ residues have $n - 1$ bonds, and $n - 1$ water molecules are lost in forming them.

Example: a tripeptide has 2 peptide bonds.
cards.searchQuery: number of peptide bonds in polypeptide n minus 1

cards.title: Which reagent labels the N-terminal residue in Edman degradation? (name or abbreviation)
cards.body:
Phenyl isothiocyanate (PITC)

PITC reacts with the free N-terminal amino group under mildly basic conditions. Mild acid then cleaves off that one residue as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) amino acid, which is identified by chromatography.

Why: the rest of the peptide stays intact, so the cycle can be repeated for sequencing.
Watch out: Edman works from the N-terminus and fails if the N-terminus is blocked, such as by acetylation.
cards.searchQuery: Edman degradation phenyl isothiocyanate N-terminal sequencing

cards.title: Which protease cleaves on the carboxyl side of Lys and Arg (but not before Pro)?
cards.body:
Trypsin

Its specificity pocket has an Asp residue that binds the positively charged Lys or Arg side chain.

Example: trypsin digestion gives predictable peptides, which is why it is the standard protease in protein mass spectrometry.
Watch out: a Lys or Arg followed by proline is not cut.
cards.searchQuery: trypsin cleaves lysine arginine carboxyl side

cards.title: Cyanogen bromide (CNBr) cleaves a peptide chain on the carboxyl side of which residue?
cards.body:
Methionine

The sulfur attacks CNBr, and the carbonyl then cyclizes, leaving a C-terminal homoserine lactone on the upstream fragment.

Tip: a protein with $n$ Met residues gives $n + 1$ fragments, which is a quick check on a digest.
cards.searchQuery: cyanogen bromide cleaves methionine peptide

cards.title: Chymotrypsin preferentially cleaves after which kind of residues?
cards.body:
Large hydrophobic (aromatic) residues: **Phe, Tyr and Trp**.

Its S1 pocket is a deep hydrophobic cleft that fits those side chains; Leu is cleaved more slowly.

Why: compare trypsin, whose pocket contains a negatively charged Asp and prefers Lys or Arg.
cards.searchQuery: chymotrypsin specificity aromatic residues Phe Tyr Trp

cards.title: Which two backbone torsion angles does a Ramachandran plot show?
cards.body:
$\phi$ (rotation about N-C$_\alpha$) and $\psi$ (rotation about C$_\alpha$-C).

Steric clashes between backbone and side-chain atoms forbid most of the plot; allowed regions correspond to $\alpha$-helices, $\beta$-strands and the left-handed helix.

Watch out: $\omega$, the angle about the peptide bond itself, is fixed near $180^\circ$ (trans), so it is not plotted.
Example: glycine, with no side chain, has a much larger allowed region.
cards.searchQuery: Ramachandran plot phi psi angles allowed regions

cards.title: How many amino acid residues are there per turn of a right-handed $\alpha$-helix? (number only)
cards.body:
3.6

The rise is $1.5\,\mathrm{\AA}$ per residue, so one turn (the pitch) is $3.6 \times 1.5 = 5.4\,\mathrm{\AA}$.

Key idea: side chains point outward, and residues $i$ and $i+3$ or $i+4$ lie on the same face, which gives amphipathic helices their pattern.
cards.searchQuery: alpha helix 3.6 residues per turn pitch 5.4 angstrom

cards.title: An ideal $\alpha$-helix rises $0.15$ nm per residue. How long, in nm, is a helix of $30$ residues? (number only)
cards.body:
4.5

$30 \times 0.15\,\mathrm{nm} = 4.5\,\mathrm{nm}$.

Example: a helix of about 25 residues, roughly 3.75 nm, is long enough to span a lipid bilayer's hydrophobic core of about 3 nm.
cards.searchQuery: alpha helix length rise per residue 0.15 nm calculation

cards.title: In an $\alpha$-helix, the C=O of residue $i$ hydrogen-bonds to the N-H of which residue?
cards.body:
Residue $i + 4$

The bonds run nearly parallel to the helix axis and enclose a ring of 13 atoms, so the helix is also called a $3.6_{13}$ helix.

Why: every backbone C=O and N-H is satisfied except at the ends, so helices are stable and the backbone is fully hydrogen-bonded.
cards.searchQuery: alpha helix hydrogen bond i to i+4 pattern

cards.title: Which $\beta$-sheet arrangement has nearly linear, stronger backbone hydrogen bonds: parallel or antiparallel?
cards.body:
Antiparallel

In an antiparallel sheet the N-H and C=O line up directly across from each other. In a parallel sheet the bonds are angled, so they are slightly longer and weaker.

Why: strands in a parallel sheet need loops that cross over, so parallel sheets are rarely just two strands and are usually buried in the core.
Key idea: a strand is nearly extended, rising about $3.3$ to $3.5\,\mathrm{\AA}$ per residue.
cards.searchQuery: antiparallel beta sheet hydrogen bonds stronger than parallel

cards.title: Which two residues are most common in tight $\beta$-turns?
cards.body:
Glycine and proline

Proline's fixed kink suits position 2, and glycine's flexibility fits the sterically crowded position 3.

Why: a $\beta$-turn reverses the chain over four residues, and the C=O of residue $i$ hydrogen-bonds to the N-H of residue $i+3$.
cards.searchQuery: beta turn glycine proline residues

cards.title: What is the main driving force for protein folding in water?
cards.body:
The **hydrophobic effect**: burying nonpolar side chains in the core.

Ordered water around exposed nonpolar groups is released, so the entropy of the solvent increases.

Why: the folded state's total stability is small, only about $20$ to $65\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, and the chain loses a lot of conformational entropy.
Watch out: hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts matter for specificity but contribute less net free energy than the hydrophobic effect.
cards.searchQuery: hydrophobic effect driving force protein folding entropy water

cards.title: Anfinsen showed that a denatured, reduced enzyme could spontaneously refold. Which enzyme did he use?
cards.body:
Ribonuclease A

He unfolded it in urea and $\beta$-mercaptoethanol, then removed both and the enzyme regained activity with correct disulfides.

Key idea: the **amino acid sequence** contains all the information needed for the native fold.
cards.searchQuery: Anfinsen ribonuclease A refolding experiment

cards.title: What is Levinthal's paradox?
cards.body:
A protein could not fold by random search of all conformations, yet it folds in milliseconds to seconds.

With about three states per residue, a 100-residue chain has roughly $3^{100}$ conformations, far too many to sample.

Why: folding follows a **funneled energy landscape**, with local structure forming early and guiding the chain downhill.
cards.searchQuery: Levinthal paradox protein folding funnel energy landscape

cards.title: Which E. coli chaperonin system, consisting of a barrel and a lid, encloses unfolded proteins in an isolated chamber so they can fold?
cards.body:
GroEL/GroES

GroEL is a double-ring barrel, and GroES caps it. ATP hydrolysis drives cycles of binding and release.

Why: the chamber prevents aggregation with other unfolded chains.
Key idea: **Hsp70** (DnaK in bacteria) is the other main chaperone class; it binds exposed hydrophobic stretches of nascent chains.
cards.searchQuery: GroEL GroES chaperonin protein folding chamber

cards.title: Which enzyme catalyzes disulfide bond exchange so that proteins reach the correct disulfide pairing in the ER?
cards.body:
Protein disulfide isomerase (PDI)

It breaks incorrect disulfides and forms new ones until the most stable pairing is found.

Why: random oxidation of eight cysteines in ribonuclease A could give 105 pairings, only one of which is native.
cards.searchQuery: protein disulfide isomerase PDI endoplasmic reticulum folding

cards.title: What is the difference in action between urea and $\beta$-mercaptoethanol when denaturing a protein?
cards.body:
Urea disrupts **noncovalent** interactions (hydrogen bonds and the hydrophobic effect); $\beta$-mercaptoethanol (or DTT) **reduces disulfide bonds**.

To fully unfold a disulfide-containing protein you usually need both.

Example: heat, extreme pH, detergents and guanidinium chloride are other denaturants that act on noncovalent forces.
cards.searchQuery: urea beta-mercaptoethanol denaturation noncovalent disulfide

cards.title: In the repeating Gly-X-Y sequence of collagen, which residue sits at every third position?
cards.body:
Glycine

Three left-handed polyproline-II-like chains wind into a right-handed triple helix. Every third residue lies in the crowded center, where only glycine's hydrogen fits.

Why: replacing Gly with a larger residue disrupts packing, as in **osteogenesis imperfecta**.
Example: X and Y are often proline and 4-hydroxyproline.
cards.searchQuery: collagen triple helix glycine every third residue

cards.title: What conformational change underlies prion diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
cards.body:
A normal, helix-rich cellular prion protein ($\mathrm{PrP^C}$) refolds into a $\beta$-sheet-rich, protease-resistant form ($\mathrm{PrP^{Sc}}$).

The misfolded form acts as a template, converting more normal protein and forming aggregates.

Key idea: an infectious agent here has **no nucleic acid**; its "information" is the protein conformation.
cards.searchQuery: prion PrPSc misfolding beta sheet template conversion

cards.title: How many $\ce{O2}$ molecules can one adult hemoglobin tetramer bind at most? (number only)
cards.body:
4

Adult Hb is $\alpha_2\beta_2$, and each of the four subunits carries one heme with an $\ce{Fe^2+}$ that binds one $\ce{O2}$.

Compare: myoglobin is a monomer and binds only one.
cards.searchQuery: hemoglobin binds four oxygen molecules alpha2 beta2

cards.title: Why is a sigmoidal oxygen-binding curve more useful for hemoglobin than a hyperbolic one?
cards.body:
Hb binds $\ce{O2}$ almost fully in the lungs (high $p_{\ce{O2}}$) and releases much of it in the tissues, where $p_{\ce{O2}}$ drops, over a narrow pressure range.

A hyperbolic curve, like that of myoglobin, would release little oxygen in the same range.

Why: cooperativity makes the curve steep near the physiological range, so a small drop in $p_{\ce{O2}}$ unloads a lot of $\ce{O2}$.
Example: Mb ($P_{50} \approx 2.8$ torr) holds on to $\ce{O2}$ until muscle is very oxygen-poor.
cards.searchQuery: hemoglobin sigmoidal curve cooperativity vs myoglobin hyperbolic

cards.title: What is the Hill coefficient $n_H$ for myoglobin binding $\ce{O2}$? (number only)
cards.body:
1

Myoglobin has a single binding site, so there is no cooperativity.

For hemoglobin $n_H \approx 2.8$ (the maximum would be $4$, from four fully cooperative sites).

Key idea: $n_H > 1$ is positive cooperativity and $n_H < 1$ is negative; the Hill coefficient is a measure of cooperativity, not the actual number of sites.
cards.searchQuery: Hill coefficient myoglobin 1 hemoglobin 2.8 cooperativity

cards.title: About what $p_{\ce{O2}}$ (in torr) gives $50\%$ saturation (the $P_{50}$) for adult hemoglobin in blood? (number only)
cards.body:
26

Hemoglobin's $P_{50}$ is about $26$ torr (mmHg), compared with about $2.8$ torr for myoglobin, so Mb has the higher oxygen affinity.

Why: lower $P_{50}$ means higher affinity; a right-shifted curve (higher $P_{50}$) means Hb releases oxygen more easily.
cards.searchQuery: hemoglobin P50 26 torr oxygen affinity

cards.title: Which hemoglobin conformation has the lower oxygen affinity: the T state or the R state?
cards.body:
The **T (tense)** state

T is stabilized by salt bridges between subunits; the **R (relaxed)** state binds $\ce{O2}$ much more tightly.

Why: binding $\ce{O2}$ to a subunit breaks some salt bridges and tips the tetramer toward R, raising the affinity of the remaining subunits.
Mnemonic: **T**ense = **T**ough to bind; **R**elaxed = **R**eady to bind.
cards.searchQuery: hemoglobin T state R state oxygen affinity salt bridges

cards.title: Which small molecule binds in the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin and lowers its oxygen affinity?
cards.body:
2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)

Its negative charges bind positive residues in the cavity between the two $\beta$ chains, which stabilizes the T state.

Example: at high altitude red cells make more BPG, shifting the curve right so more $\ce{O2}$ is released in tissues.
Watch out: BPG fits only in the deoxy (T) form, because the cavity narrows in R.
cards.searchQuery: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate hemoglobin oxygen affinity T state

cards.title: What does the Bohr effect say about the effect of lower pH or higher $\ce{CO2}$ on hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?
cards.body:
It **decreases** the affinity (right shift).

$\ce{H+}$ protonates certain residues (such as His146 of the $\beta$ chain), which strengthens the salt bridges of the T state; $\ce{CO2}$ also lowers pH and forms carbamates.

Why: active tissue makes $\ce{CO2}$ and acid, so Hb releases more $\ce{O2}$ where it is needed.
Key idea: the reverse also holds; in the lungs, $\ce{CO2}$ leaves, pH rises and Hb loads $\ce{O2}$.
cards.searchQuery: Bohr effect hemoglobin pH CO2 oxygen affinity right shift

cards.title: Why does fetal hemoglobin ($\alpha_2\gamma_2$) have a higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin?
cards.body:
It binds 2,3-BPG **less tightly**.

The $\gamma$ chain has a serine in place of the histidine at position 143 of the $\beta$ chain, so one positive charge of the BPG-binding site is missing.

Why: the higher affinity lets the fetus take $\ce{O2}$ from maternal blood across the placenta.
cards.searchQuery: fetal hemoglobin HbF lower BPG binding higher oxygen affinity

cards.title: How is the heme iron coordinated in oxymyoglobin, and what role does the distal histidine play?
cards.body:
Four bonds to the porphyrin nitrogens, a fifth to the **proximal His** (F8), and $\ce{O2}$ as the sixth ligand.

The **distal His** (E7) hydrogen-bonds to the bound $\ce{O2}$ and sterically bends bound CO.

Why: that reduces CO binding from about $20{,}000$ times tighter than $\ce{O2}$ in free heme to about $200$ times in globins.
Watch out: iron stays $\ce{Fe^2+}$ in oxygenated hemoglobin; $\ce{O2}$ does not oxidize it.
cards.searchQuery: heme iron proximal distal histidine oxygen binding myoglobin

cards.title: What is methemoglobin, and why can it not carry oxygen?
cards.body:
Hemoglobin whose heme iron has been oxidized from $\ce{Fe^2+}$ to $\ce{Fe^3+}$.

The ferric form cannot bind $\ce{O2}$.

Example: nitrites and some drugs cause methemoglobinemia; the enzyme **methemoglobin reductase** (NADH-dependent) normally keeps the level under about $1\%$.
Tip: blood looks chocolate brown in methemoglobinemia, and patients appear cyanotic.
cards.searchQuery: methemoglobin Fe3+ cannot bind oxygen methemoglobin reductase

cards.title: How does the Glu6Val substitution in the $\beta$ chain cause hemoglobin S to polymerize?
cards.body:
Valine creates a **hydrophobic patch** on the surface of deoxyHb S that fits into a pocket on another molecule.

Only the deoxy form has that pocket, so fibers form when $\ce{O2}$ is low and distort the red cell.

Why: glutamate is charged and soluble, while valine is nonpolar and drives stickiness.
Watch out: this is a surface mutation that changes solubility and not oxygen-binding itself.
cards.searchQuery: sickle cell hemoglobin S Glu6Val hydrophobic patch polymerization

cards.title: Which cooperativity model proposes that all subunits switch together between T and R states?
cards.body:
The concerted model (Monod-Wyman-Changeux, MWC)

It says the tetramer exists in a T $\rightleftharpoons$ R equilibrium and is always symmetric; $\ce{O2}$ binding shifts the equilibrium toward R.

Watch out: the **sequential** (Koshland-Nemethy-Filmer) model lets subunits change one at a time. Real Hb behaves in between.
cards.searchQuery: MWC concerted model cooperativity hemoglobin sequential KNF

cards.title: What structural change at the heme starts the T to R transition when $\ce{O2}$ binds?
cards.body:
The iron moves into the plane of the porphyrin ring, pulling the proximal histidine and its helix.

In deoxyHb the high-spin $\ce{Fe^2+}$ sits slightly out of the plane; oxygen binding makes it low-spin and slightly smaller so it fits.

Why: the pull on helix F is passed to the subunit interface and breaks salt bridges, favoring R.
cards.searchQuery: hemoglobin heme iron moves into plane oxygen binding T to R

cards.title: What two thermodynamic quantities does an enzyme leave unchanged?
cards.body:
$\Delta G$ (overall free energy change) and $K_{eq}$.

Enzymes lower the **activation energy** and speed up both the forward and reverse reactions equally.

Why: the free energies of reactants and products are state functions, so catalysts cannot change them.
Watch out: an enzyme cannot make a reaction with $\Delta G > 0$ proceed spontaneously.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme does not change Keq or delta G activation energy

cards.title: Why are transition-state analogs such potent enzyme inhibitors?
cards.body:
Enzymes bind the **transition state** more tightly than the substrate, so a stable molecule that mimics it binds extremely tightly.

Example: oseltamivir (Tamiflu) resembles the transition state of neuraminidase as a mimic of the sialic acid cleavage intermediate.

Key idea: catalysis comes mostly from tight binding of the transition state, not the substrate.
cards.searchQuery: transition state analog inhibitor enzyme tight binding

cards.title: At what rate does an enzyme obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics turn over when $[S] = K_m$?
cards.body:
$V_{max}/2$

Plug in: $v_0 = \frac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]} = \frac{V_{max} K_m}{2 K_m} = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$.

Key idea: $K_m$ is the substrate concentration at half-maximal rate, and it is in concentration units.
Watch out: $K_m$ equals the dissociation constant $K_d$ only when $k_{cat} \ll k_{-1}$.
cards.searchQuery: Michaelis constant Km substrate concentration half Vmax

cards.title: $V_{max} = 100\,\mu\mathrm{M/min}$ and $K_m = 2\,\mathrm{mM}$. What is $v_0$, in $\mu\mathrm{M/min}$, at $[S] = 6\,\mathrm{mM}$? (number only)
cards.body:
75

$v_0 = \frac{100 \times 6}{2 + 6} = \frac{600}{8} = 75\,\mu\mathrm{M/min}$.

Tip: keep $[S]$ and $K_m$ in the same units; the ratio matters, so mM works without converting.
cards.searchQuery: Michaelis-Menten equation calculate initial velocity

cards.title: What substrate concentration, as a multiple of $K_m$, gives $90\%$ of $V_{max}$? (number only)
cards.body:
9

$0.9 = \frac{[S]}{K_m + [S]}$ gives $0.9 K_m = 0.1 [S]$, so $[S] = 9 K_m$.

Why: the curve approaches $V_{max}$ slowly, which is why you cannot measure $V_{max}$ directly and instead fit the curve.
Tip: $[S] = 19 K_m$ gives $95\%$.
cards.searchQuery: substrate concentration 90 percent Vmax 9 Km

cards.title: An assay gives $V_{max} = 120\,\mu\mathrm{M/min}$ with total enzyme $[E]_t = 0.5\,\mu\mathrm{M}$. What is $k_{cat}$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$? (number only)
cards.body:
4

$k_{cat} = V_{max}/[E]_t = 120/0.5 = 240\,\mathrm{min^{-1}} = 4\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

Watch out: convert minutes to seconds; $k_{cat}$ is the turnover number, the number of substrate molecules converted per active site per second.
cards.searchQuery: kcat turnover number calculation Vmax enzyme concentration

cards.title: Which ratio, in units of $\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$, measures an enzyme's catalytic efficiency and specificity for a substrate?
cards.body:
$k_{cat}/K_m$

It is the second-order rate constant at low $[S]$, where $v_0 \approx \frac{k_{cat}}{K_m}[E][S]$.

Key idea: the upper limit is set by diffusion, about $10^8$ to $10^9\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$; enzymes near it, like triose phosphate isomerase, are called **catalytically perfect**.
Tip: compare $k_{cat}/K_m$ across substrates to see which one an enzyme prefers.
cards.searchQuery: kcat/Km catalytic efficiency diffusion limit enzyme

cards.title: What are the slope and intercepts of a Lineweaver-Burk plot of $1/v_0$ versus $1/[S]$?
cards.body:
Slope $= K_m/V_{max}$; y-intercept $= 1/V_{max}$; x-intercept $= -1/K_m$.

It comes from inverting Michaelis-Menten: $\frac{1}{v_0} = \frac{K_m}{V_{max}}\frac{1}{[S]} + \frac{1}{V_{max}}$.

Watch out: the points at low $[S]$ are weighted heavily and carry the most error, so nonlinear fitting is better for real data. The plot is mainly for diagnosing inhibition type.
cards.searchQuery: Lineweaver-Burk plot slope intercept Km Vmax double reciprocal

cards.title: A Lineweaver-Burk plot has an x-intercept of $-0.5\,\mathrm{mM^{-1}}$. What is $K_m$ in mM? (number only)
cards.body:
2

The x-intercept is $-1/K_m$, so $K_m = 1/0.5 = 2\,\mathrm{mM}$.

Example: with a y-intercept of $0.02\,(\mu\mathrm{M/min})^{-1}$, $V_{max} = 1/0.02 = 50\,\mu\mathrm{M/min}$.
cards.searchQuery: Lineweaver-Burk x-intercept negative reciprocal Km calculation

cards.title: An inhibitor raises the apparent $K_m$ but leaves $V_{max}$ unchanged. What type of reversible inhibition is this?
cards.body:
Competitive inhibition

The inhibitor binds the free enzyme at the active site and competes with substrate; enough substrate overcomes it.

Why: $V_{max}$ is reached at saturating $[S]$, where the inhibitor is outcompeted; $K_m$ appears larger because more substrate is needed to reach half-maximum.
Example: malonate competes with succinate at succinate dehydrogenase.
cards.searchQuery: competitive inhibition Km increases Vmax unchanged

cards.title: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds E and ES with equal affinity. What happens to $V_{max}$ and $K_m$?
cards.body:
$V_{max}$ **decreases**; $K_m$ is **unchanged**.

The inhibitor removes active enzyme from the pool, which behaves like having less enzyme, and substrate binding is unaffected.

Why: on a Lineweaver-Burk plot the lines meet on the x-axis at $-1/K_m$, with a larger y-intercept.
Watch out: pure noncompetitive inhibition is rare; most noncompetitive inhibitors are really **mixed** (they bind E and ES with different affinity), which also changes $K_m$.
cards.searchQuery: noncompetitive inhibition Vmax decreases Km unchanged

cards.title: An inhibitor binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex. How do $V_{max}$ and $K_m$ change?
cards.body:
Both **decrease** by the same factor, which is uncompetitive inhibition.

Lineweaver-Burk lines are **parallel**, with the same slope $K_m/V_{max}$ but a higher intercept.

Why: binding to ES pulls substrate binding forward (Le Chatelier), lowering the apparent $K_m$, while the dead-end ESI complex lowers $V_{max}$.
Example: lithium inhibition of inositol monophosphatase is the classic example.
cards.searchQuery: uncompetitive inhibition parallel lines Vmax and Km decrease

cards.title: How does mixed inhibition appear on a Lineweaver-Burk plot?
cards.body:
The lines intersect to the **left of the y-axis**, so $V_{max}$ falls and $K_m$ changes.

The inhibitor binds both E and ES, but with different affinities ($K_i \ne K_i'$).

Key idea: if $K_i < K_i'$ (prefers E), $K_m$ rises; if $K_i > K_i'$ (prefers ES), $K_m$ falls. Pure noncompetitive is the special case $K_i = K_i'$.
cards.searchQuery: mixed inhibition Lineweaver-Burk lines intersect

cards.title: $K_m = 2\,\mathrm{mM}$. A competitive inhibitor at $10\,\mu\mathrm{M}$ has $K_i = 5\,\mu\mathrm{M}$. What is the apparent $K_m$ in mM? (number only)
cards.body:
6

$K_m^{app} = K_m\left(1 + \frac{[I]}{K_i}\right) = 2 \times (1 + 2) = 6\,\mathrm{mM}$.

Watch out: $V_{max}$ is unchanged for a competitive inhibitor; only $K_m$ is scaled up by the factor $\alpha = 1 + [I]/K_i$.
cards.searchQuery: apparent Km competitive inhibitor Ki calculation

cards.title: Where do Lineweaver-Burk lines with and without a competitive inhibitor intersect?
cards.body:
On the **y-axis** at $1/V_{max}$.

The y-intercept is unchanged, while the slope and x-intercept change because $K_m^{app}$ rises.

Tip: **C**ompetitive lines **C**ross on the y-axis (same $V_{max}$); noncompetitive lines cross on the x-axis (same $K_m$).
cards.searchQuery: competitive inhibition Lineweaver-Burk lines intersect y-axis

cards.title: Name an irreversible inhibitor that covalently modifies the active-site serine of acetylcholinesterase and serine proteases.
cards.body:
Diisopropylfluorophosphate (DFP), a nerve-agent-like organophosphate.

It phosphorylates the catalytic Ser, and the enzyme cannot be regenerated on a useful timescale.

Example: aspirin acetylates a serine in cyclooxygenase, and penicillin acylates the transpeptidase serine in bacterial cell wall synthesis.
cards.searchQuery: DFP irreversible inhibitor serine protease acetylcholinesterase

cards.title: Why must Michaelis-Menten kinetics be measured as an initial rate with $[S] \gg [E]$?
cards.body:
So that $[S]$ stays essentially constant and product has not accumulated enough for the reverse reaction or product inhibition to matter.

The model assumes a **steady state**: $[ES]$ stays constant over the measurement, since the rate of formation equals the rate of breakdown.

Why: once much substrate is used or substantial product forms, the measured rate no longer reflects $[S]_0$.
Tip: keep conversion under about $10\%$ of the substrate.
cards.searchQuery: Michaelis-Menten steady state assumption initial velocity substrate excess

cards.title: How does an allosteric enzyme's rate-versus-$[S]$ curve differ from a Michaelis-Menten enzyme's?
cards.body:
It is **sigmoidal**, not hyperbolic, because of cooperativity between subunits.

The substrate concentration at half $V_{max}$ is written $K_{0.5}$ (or $S_{0.5}$), not $K_m$.

Why: an allosteric activator shifts the curve left (lower $K_{0.5}$); an inhibitor shifts it right and makes it more sigmoidal.
Key idea: allosteric enzymes do not obey the Michaelis-Menten equation, so $K_m$ is not defined.
cards.searchQuery: allosteric enzyme sigmoidal kinetics K0.5 cooperativity

cards.title: Which nucleotide is the feedback inhibitor of aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase)?
cards.body:
CTP

ATCase makes N-carbamoylaspartate from carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate, the committed step of pyrimidine synthesis. CTP (the end product) stabilizes the T state; ATP stabilizes R.

Why: ATP activation signals that purines are plentiful, balancing the two nucleotide pools.
Key idea: ATCase is the classic allosteric enzyme, built from 6 catalytic and 6 regulatory subunits.
cards.searchQuery: ATCase aspartate transcarbamoylase CTP feedback inhibition

cards.title: What is an inactive precursor of an enzyme, activated by proteolytic cleavage, called?
cards.body:
A zymogen (proenzyme)

Example: trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by enteropeptidase, and trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen and other zymogens.

Why: it lets digestive enzymes be stored and secreted without digesting the cells that make them.
Watch out: this is irreversible, unlike phosphorylation.
cards.searchQuery: zymogen proenzyme trypsinogen proteolytic activation

cards.title: In the catalytic triad of chymotrypsin (Asp102, His57, Ser195), which residue is the nucleophile that attacks the peptide carbonyl?
cards.body:
Serine (Ser195)

His57 acts as a general base that pulls the proton from Ser195, and Asp102 orients and stabilizes the protonated His.

Key idea: this forms a covalent **acyl-enzyme** intermediate, and then water (activated by His) hydrolyzes it.
Watch out: the Ser is nucleophilic only because of the triad; free serine is not very reactive.
cards.searchQuery: chymotrypsin catalytic triad serine nucleophile

cards.title: What is the role of the oxyanion hole in serine proteases?
cards.body:
It stabilizes the negatively charged oxygen of the **tetrahedral intermediate** by hydrogen bonds from backbone N-H groups.

This lowers the energy of the transition state, which resembles that intermediate.

Why: the hole fits the tetrahedral geometry better than the planar substrate, so it helps only once the transition state is reached.
cards.searchQuery: oxyanion hole serine protease tetrahedral intermediate stabilization

cards.title: What did the "burst" of product release seen with chymotrypsin and $p$-nitrophenyl acetate reveal?
cards.body:
A two-step mechanism: fast **acylation** (releasing the first product) and then slow **deacylation**.

The burst size equals the amount of active enzyme, which also allows active-site titration.

Why: if deacylation is rate-limiting, the acyl-enzyme builds up and the steady-state rate is lower than the initial burst.
cards.searchQuery: chymotrypsin burst kinetics acyl-enzyme p-nitrophenyl acetate

cards.title: To which EC enzyme class do kinases belong?
cards.body:
Transferases (EC 2)

Kinases transfer a phosphoryl group from ATP to a substrate.

The seven classes: **1** oxidoreductases, **2** transferases, **3** hydrolases, **4** lyases, **5** isomerases, **6** ligases and **7** translocases (added in 2018).
Example: hexokinase is EC 2.7.1.1; the 2.7 means phosphotransferases.
cards.searchQuery: EC enzyme classification kinase transferase class

cards.title: Which EC enzyme class joins two molecules using energy from ATP hydrolysis?
cards.body:
Ligases (EC 6), also called synthetases

They form C-C, C-O, C-N or C-S bonds coupled to ATP (or similar) cleavage.

Example: DNA ligase seals nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone of DNA.
Watch out: do not confuse them with **lyases** (EC 4), which add or remove groups to form double bonds without ATP, or **synthases**, which do not require ATP.
cards.searchQuery: ligase EC 6 ATP joins two molecules synthetase

cards.title: List the main catalytic strategies enzymes use to lower activation energy.
cards.body:
- General acid-base catalysis
- Covalent catalysis
- Metal-ion catalysis
- Proximity and orientation of substrates
- Preferential binding of the transition state

Example: chymotrypsin uses covalent catalysis (Ser195), general base catalysis (His57), and transition-state stabilization (oxyanion hole).
Key idea: most enzymes combine several of these at once.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme catalytic mechanisms acid base covalent metal ion proximity

cards.title: Which metal ion in the active site of carbonic anhydrase activates a bound water molecule?
cards.body:
Zinc ($\ce{Zn^2+}$)

The zinc lowers the pKa of its bound water so that hydroxide is present at neutral pH, and the hydroxide attacks $\ce{CO2}$ to give bicarbonate.

Key idea: carbonic anhydrase is one of the fastest enzymes known, with $k_{cat}$ around $10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
cards.searchQuery: carbonic anhydrase zinc active site water hydroxide

cards.title: Which vitamin-derived cofactor carries activated $\ce{CO2}$ in carboxylation reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase?
cards.body:
Biotin

It is covalently attached to a lysine of the enzyme and carries $\ce{CO2}$ on one of its ring nitrogens, using ATP to activate bicarbonate.

Why: dietary deficiency is rare, but raw egg whites contain **avidin**, which binds biotin extremely tightly.
cards.searchQuery: biotin carboxylase cofactor carbon dioxide carrier

cards.title: Which common hexose is the C4 epimer of D-glucose?
cards.body:
Galactose

Epimers differ in configuration at exactly one stereocenter. D-Mannose is the C2 epimer of glucose.

Example: galactose in lactose is converted to glucose by an epimerase after it is activated as UDP-galactose.
Watch out: epimers are diastereomers, not enantiomers.
cards.searchQuery: galactose C4 epimer of glucose epimers

cards.title: When a sugar cyclizes into a hemiacetal or hemiketal ring, the new stereocenter is called what kind of carbon?
cards.body:
The **anomeric carbon**

It is C1 in aldoses and C2 in ketoses such as fructose. The two forms are the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ anomers.

Why: in D-glucopyranose, $\beta$ has the anomeric $\ce{-OH}$ on the same side as the $\ce{CH2OH}$ group (up in Haworth); $\alpha$ has it opposite (down).
Key idea: **mutarotation** interconverts the anomers in water through the open-chain form, giving about $64\%$ $\beta$ and $36\%$ $\alpha$ at equilibrium.
cards.searchQuery: anomeric carbon alpha beta anomers glucose mutarotation

cards.title: How many stereoisomers does an open-chain aldohexose have? (number only)
cards.body:
16

An aldohexose has four chiral centers (C2 to C5), so there are $2^4 = 16$ stereoisomers, 8 of them D and 8 L.

Why: a ketohexose has only three chiral centers, so it has $2^3 = 8$.
Tip: the D or L label comes from the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl (C5 in hexoses).
cards.searchQuery: aldohexose number of stereoisomers 2^n chiral centers

cards.title: Which common disaccharide is non-reducing because the anomeric carbons of both sugars are tied up in its glycosidic bond?
cards.body:
Sucrose

It is glucose and fructose joined $\alpha(1\rightarrow\beta 2)$, which uses both anomeric carbons.

Compare: lactose (Gal $\beta(1\rightarrow4)$ Glc) and maltose (Glc $\alpha(1\rightarrow4)$ Glc) keep a free anomeric carbon on one residue, so they are reducing sugars.
Why: a reducing sugar can open its ring to expose an aldehyde that reduces $\ce{Cu^2+}$ in Benedict's test.
cards.searchQuery: sucrose nonreducing disaccharide anomeric carbon glycosidic bond

cards.title: Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose, even though both are glucose polymers?
cards.body:
Starch has $\alpha(1\rightarrow4)$ linkages, which amylase cleaves; cellulose has $\beta(1\rightarrow4)$ linkages, which human enzymes cannot cleave.

The $\beta$ linkage flips every other glucose, producing straight chains that H-bond into rigid fibrils; $\alpha$ linkages give a helical, compact coil.

Example: ruminants and termites rely on gut microbes that make cellulase.
cards.searchQuery: starch alpha 1-4 cellulose beta 1-4 linkage digestion

cards.title: How do glycogen and amylopectin differ in branching frequency?
cards.body:
Glycogen has an $\alpha(1\rightarrow6)$ branch about every $8$ to $12$ residues; amylopectin about every $24$ to $30$.

Why: more branches mean more non-reducing ends, so glycogen can be mobilized quickly by many phosphorylase molecules working at once.
Key idea: both branch points are $\alpha(1\rightarrow6)$ linkages, while the chains are $\alpha(1\rightarrow4)$.
cards.searchQuery: glycogen amylopectin branching frequency alpha 1-6 linkage

cards.title: N-linked glycosylation attaches a glycan to the side chain of which amino acid?
cards.body:
Asparagine, within the sequon Asn-X-Ser/Thr (X is any residue except Pro).

This occurs in the ER, starting from a lipid-linked precursor ($\ce{Glc3Man9GlcNAc2}$-dolichol).

Compare: O-linked glycans are attached to the $\ce{-OH}$ of Ser or Thr, typically in the Golgi, one sugar at a time.
cards.searchQuery: N-linked glycosylation asparagine sequon Asn-X-Ser/Thr

cards.title: Which essential $\omega$-3 fatty acid is $18{:}3(\Delta^{9,12,15})$?
cards.body:
$\alpha$-Linolenic acid (ALA)

Humans lack desaturases that put double bonds beyond $\Delta^9$, so they must get ALA and linoleic acid ($18{:}2$, $\omega$-6) from the diet.

Why: ALA is the precursor to EPA and DHA, though human conversion is limited.
Example: flax and walnuts are rich in ALA.
cards.searchQuery: alpha-linolenic acid omega-3 essential fatty acid 18:3

cards.title: Why do unsaturated fatty acids with cis double bonds have lower melting points than saturated ones?
cards.body:
A cis double bond puts a rigid **kink** in the chain, so the tails cannot pack tightly and van der Waals contacts are fewer.

Example: stearic acid ($18{:}0$) melts near $70\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while oleic acid ($18{:}1$ cis) melts near $13\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
Watch out: trans fats lack the kink, so they pack like saturated fats.
cards.searchQuery: cis double bond kink fatty acid melting point packing

cards.title: How does cholesterol act as a fluidity buffer in animal cell membranes?
cards.body:
At high temperature it **restricts** the motion of fatty acid tails; at low temperature it **prevents** tight packing and crystallization.

Its rigid steroid ring lies next to the first carbons of the tails, and its small polar $\ce{-OH}$ group sits at the aqueous surface.

Key idea: cholesterol broadens the phase transition so the membrane stays fluid but not leaky.
cards.searchQuery: cholesterol membrane fluidity buffer temperature

cards.title: Why is transverse (flip-flop) diffusion of membrane lipids slow compared with lateral diffusion?
cards.body:
A lipid must drag its polar head group through the hydrophobic core, a high energy barrier; lateral movement keeps heads in the aqueous surface.

Flip-flop happens over hours to days unless catalyzed by **flippases**, floppases or scramblases.

Example: flippases keep phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet; its exposure on the outer leaflet signals apoptosis.
cards.searchQuery: membrane lipid flip-flop slow flippase lateral diffusion

cards.title: For each ATP hydrolyzed, how many $\ce{Na+}$ ions does the $\ce{Na+}/\ce{K+}$-ATPase pump out of the cell? (number only)
cards.body:
3

The pump moves $3\,\ce{Na+}$ out and $2\,\ce{K+}$ in per ATP, so it makes the membrane potential more negative inside.

Why: it is a P-type ATPase, forming a phospho-aspartate intermediate and cycling between E1 and E2 conformations.
Key idea: **cardiac glycosides** such as digoxin inhibit it.
cards.searchQuery: sodium potassium ATPase 3 Na out 2 K in per ATP

cards.title: Which glucose transporter in muscle and fat moves to the plasma membrane in response to insulin?
cards.body:
GLUT4

Insulin signaling triggers fusion of GLUT4-containing vesicles with the membrane, and glucose enters by facilitated diffusion.

Compare: GLUT2 (liver, pancreatic $\beta$-cells) has a high $K_m$ and tracks blood glucose, while GLUT1 and GLUT3 operate constitutively.
Example: exercise also moves GLUT4 to the surface, independent of insulin.
cards.searchQuery: GLUT4 insulin glucose transporter muscle adipose

cards.title: What is the backbone of sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids, made of sphingosine plus a fatty acid?
cards.body:
Ceramide

Sphingomyelin is ceramide with a phosphocholine head; cerebrosides and gangliosides have sugar head groups instead.

Why: sphingosine is an amino alcohol, and its amide-linked fatty acid makes ceramide the structural core of this lipid family.
cards.searchQuery: ceramide sphingosine fatty acid sphingolipid backbone

cards.title: An $A_{260}$ of $1.0$ corresponds to about what concentration, in $\mu\mathrm{g/mL}$, of double-stranded DNA? (number only)
cards.body:
50

For comparison, $A_{260} = 1$ is about $40\,\mu\mathrm{g/mL}$ for RNA and $33\,\mu\mathrm{g/mL}$ for single-stranded DNA.

Tip: a pure DNA sample has $A_{260}/A_{280} \approx 1.8$ and pure RNA about $2.0$; a lower ratio suggests protein contamination.
cards.searchQuery: A260 1.0 equals 50 ug/mL double stranded DNA

cards.title: Is Z-DNA a left-handed or right-handed helix?
cards.body:
Left-handed

Z-DNA has about $12$ bp per turn and a zigzag backbone; B-DNA is right-handed with about $10.5$ bp per turn, and A-DNA is right-handed with about $11$.

Example: alternating purine-pyrimidine runs (such as CGCGCG) and high salt favor Z-DNA.
cards.searchQuery: Z-DNA left-handed helix B-DNA A-DNA comparison

cards.title: How does the GC content of a DNA molecule affect its melting temperature $T_m$, and why?
cards.body:
Higher GC content gives a **higher** $T_m$.

G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly than A-T pairs, which have two.

Why: melting also increases $A_{260}$ by about $30\%$ (the **hyperchromic effect**) as stacked bases unstack.
Tip: $T_m$ also rises with salt concentration, since cations shield backbone phosphate repulsion.
cards.searchQuery: DNA melting temperature GC content hyperchromic effect
